doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Playing with Arnett Cobb and Jimmy Ford in Houston
summary: As 'Little Eddie' he played with Arnett Cobb and older Houston musicians who protected and taught him.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: There was a mention here that you played early on with Arnett Cobb?
What was that like — not only musically but socially and generationally. How did he speak to you about what he wanted?

Oh he didn’t. I was known as “Little Eddie” because all the guys that I played with when I was coming up — Arnett was — I knew what he wanted because I did my homework and I wasn’t going to try to do my Roy Haynes imitation behind Arnett Cobb. Straight ahead, straight ahead. He was very kind, a man who endured unbelievable pain because of that horrible accident he had. How he stayed on the stage on those crutches or sitting on the stool all night, never went to the men’s room, because it was so difficult for him to get around. But that never came out in his playing or in his personality. Very, very sweet. Very supportive. There were some other guys I played with who were younger who were more — Arnett could have been my grandfather. And these other guys I played with — Jimmy Ford, the great alto player; Don Wilkerson, another great tenor player; and some really incredible Hispanic jazz musicians in Houston who were all old enough to be my dad. My father would take me to the gig and sit there and listen and they would — when the candyman came in the guys would go to the back room with the candyman and say, “Eddie, why don’t you go out and sit with your father for a while.” So they protected me from the seedier elements.

And these men that I played with were gentlemen, they were very supportive in a much different way than Arnett. I was told Jimmy would whip around and, “What in the hell are you doing back there? Building a house?” Or, “You’re playing so goddamn loud I can’t hear myself. So yeah, that’s where I learned, really. Because thank God those men cared enough, they could have just said, “Get out of here, kid.” But they helped me. They taught me how to play.
